my_sentence: I stayed at home and rest.
correction: I stayed at home and rested.
explanation: The two completed actions should use parallel past-tense verbs: "stayed" and "rested."
correct_examples: I stayed home and watched TV.
She worked all day and rested at night.

my_sentence: I don't think the rich have responsibility to help the poor.
correction: I don't think the rich have a responsibility to help the poor.
explanation: Use the article "a" before the singular count noun "responsibility."
correct_examples: Parents have a responsibility to protect children.
The company has a responsibility to its customers.
context: Discussing whether rich people must help the poor.

my_sentence: A responsibility means some duty you need to finish them by yourself.
correction: A responsibility means some duty you need to finish by yourself.
explanation: The singular noun "duty" needs the singular pronoun "it," or the object can be omitted; "them" does not agree with it.
correct_examples: A responsibility is a duty you must complete.
This is a task you need to finish yourself.

my_sentence: There are three advantages about rich people.
correction: There are three advantages for rich people.
explanation: The preposition "for" shows who receives the advantage; "about" would mean the advantages are merely about the topic.
correct_examples: There are several advantages for students.
This policy has advantages for workers.
context: Listing advantages of not having a duty to help the poor.

my_sentence: Rich people should focus their own companies.
correction: Rich people should focus on their own companies.
explanation: The verb "focus" requires the preposition "on" before its object.
correct_examples: Please focus on your work.
The team focused on customer needs.
context: Discussing how business owners spend their time.

my_sentence: You shouldn't give them other tasks to load their focus.
correction: You shouldn't give them other tasks to distract them.
explanation: The natural verb for taking attention away from a task is "distract," not "load someone's focus."
correct_examples: Noise can distract me from my work.
Extra meetings distract employees from their main tasks.
context: Explaining why busy people should not receive extra duties.

my_sentence: We can use our effort to read out of poverty.
correction: We can use our efforts to get out of poverty.
explanation: The fixed phrase is "get out of poverty," and the plural noun "efforts" fits this general statement.
correct_examples: Education can help people get out of poverty.
They used their efforts to improve their lives.

my_sentence: I don't care about others' affairs.
correction: I don't care about other people's affairs.
explanation: Use "other people's" when referring to the affairs of people in general; the possessive form needs a clear noun owner.
correct_examples: I try not to discuss other people's affairs.
She does not interfere in other people's business.

my_sentence: I don't need to be treated as a children.
correction: I don't need to be treated as a child.
explanation: After "a," use the singular count noun "child."
correct_examples: He is old enough to make his own decisions.
She does not want to be treated like a child.
context: Explaining why friends should not overprotect him.

my_sentence: In my company there are many kind of people.
correction: In my company there are many kinds of people.
explanation: After the plural quantifier "many," use the plural count noun "kinds."
correct_examples: There are many kinds of people at work.
The store sells many kinds of fruit.

my_sentence: If you meet some problems, they are willing to help you.
correction: If you meet some problems, they will be willing to help you.
explanation: Use "will be willing" for the future result of the condition.
correct_examples: If you need help, they will be willing to assist you.
If a problem occurs, my coworkers will help.
context: Explaining how coworkers support each other.

my_sentence: They can cover most of people.
correction: They can cover most of the people.
explanation: When "most of" is followed by a specific group, use the determiner "the."
correct_examples: The hospitals serve most of the people in the city.
This service helps most of the residents.

my_sentence: The basic right of live is protected by the government.
correction: The basic right to live is protected by the government.
explanation: Use the infinitive phrase "the right to live," not "the right of live."
correct_examples: Everyone has the right to live safely.
The law protects the right to work.

my_sentence: The government needs to provide safer within the environmental policy.
correction: The government needs to provide safety through environmental policies.
explanation: "Safer" is a comparative adjective; the noun needed here is "safety," and general policies are usually plural.
correct_examples: The policy provides safety for residents.
Environmental policies can protect public health.

my_sentence: If you want to see your diseases, you need to wait for a long time.
correction: If you want to see a doctor about your illness, you need to wait for a long time.
explanation: People see a doctor, not a disease; use the count noun "a doctor" for the person being visited.
correct_examples: I need to see a doctor about my illness.
She waited to see a specialist.
context: Discussing waiting times in public hospitals.

my_sentence: Most parents like to buy milk powder from other countries.
correction: Most parents like to buy milk powder from other countries, not from China.
explanation: The teacher completed the contrast with the second source; repeat the preposition to make the comparison clear.
correct_examples: Many people buy products from Japan, not from China.
They prefer milk powder from other countries.

my_sentence: I can go there to find them.
correction: I can go there to find a doctor.
explanation: After discussing hospitals, name the person being sought; "find them" is unclear because the pronoun has no clear antecedent.
correct_examples: I went to the clinic to find a doctor.
You can go there to see a specialist.
context: Explaining where to find mental-health professionals.

my_sentence: I have graduated from college many years ago.
correction: I graduated from college many years ago.
explanation: A finished event with a definite past-time expression such as "many years ago" takes the simple past, not the present perfect.
correct_examples: I graduated from college in 2010.
She moved abroad many years ago.
context: Talking about education and work history.
